name: Priya Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Our conversation is confidential. What is your usual shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 43, and I lead the die-cutting line that makes medicine cartons. A two-year technical diploma taught me tooling, but I learned the hard way to check the first fold after changing a die; a carton that looks tidy flat can spring open at packing. I like getting the print and crease to meet exactly, and I hate scraping a jam after a roll of board splits.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household picture, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Arun repairs heating systems, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is above the usual operator rate, we have around eleven months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other packaging plants nearby. I use an AI tool occasionally to read a supplier manual, after another operator has tried it, but I set the die from the written measurement and the sample carton.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the carton crew an AI order list might be tidier, but somebody still has to fold the first medicine box. I would be pleased if the small saving meant less rushed checking at the end of a roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The die-cutting job looks sound and the pay is good, while Arun's heating work has regular customers. Eleven months saved and several nearby plants give us room if this employer has a slow patch. I would still want to know whether the first-fold test stays on the paid schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the die and folding the first carton from every new roll. From each full paid month I would add a small new amount to our home repair account; I would keep using the manual search only when a page is hard to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. An order list can be dull or clever, but I am paid to make a box that stays shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which check catches a bad carton?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I fold the first carton and tug the glued seam before a whole roll goes through. Last week the print looked perfect, but the crease split under my thumb. A perfect medicine-carton print cannot hold a split crease together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the home repair account for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our roof needs a small repair before winter, and I want to pay it from new wages rather than dip into the income reserve. If a full month is not paid, I would skip that month's extra deposit.

say: I would tell colleagues **first-fold checks** still matter when software tidies carton orders.
I would ask the plant to keep **paid inspection time** at each new roll.
think: Our **high operator pay** and eleven-month reserve make this mild picture secure.
Several **nearby plants** give us options if packaging orders slow.
do: **Keep** setting carton dies and folding the first box from each roll.
**Add** newly earned full-month wages to the roof repair account.
feel: **Calm** about work and money while insisting on an honest carton check.
S0.quote: A perfect medicine-carton print cannot hold a split crease together.
fieldNote: Her **first-fold check** has a specific defect behind it: the crease split despite clean printing.
The **roof deposit** is new pay from full months, separate from eleven months already reserved for income gaps.

steps.text: Keep setting carton dies and checking first fold each roll
Save fresh full-month wages for roof repair if paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop that AI can write schedules and order board before a robot can clear a split roll. I would ask management for the planned paid setup hours and an actual machine test, because a press release cannot show where the jam happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose some lead hours if one person is made to cover two cutters after the new camera arrives. Arun's heating wage and our savings help, but I do not want to burn that cushion because someone calls a smaller roster efficient. I would wait for a working line before trusting the sales figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the proposed roster with four recent pay slips and ask another plant's lead how its camera worked on a full shift. If our employer offers a funded paid practical place on the new cutter controls with a trainer and guarded test rolls, I would take it. If my base hours are cut, I would apply only to posted nearby packaging lead posts with safe duties, a base wage and shifts that fit our bills and the children's pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible reduction in my own hours, despite the reserve. I can handle a new control once somebody has shown that it works on board, not just on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guarded trial have to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera must catch a bad crease, and I need to stop the cutter without reaching across moving board. A trainer should watch the first test on a waste roll before we feed medicine cartons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any nearby plant pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a posted base rate that covers the mortgage and a shift ending before school pickup. There are factories nearby, but I will not leave a good wage for an overtime estimate.

say: I would ask for **written setup hours** before trusting a new camera target.
A **guarded waste-roll test** should prove the cutter can stop safely.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink if one operator covers two cutters.
Arun's wage and our **strong reserve** give time, but do not make a cut harmless.
do: **Compare** proposed setup hours with four wage slips and a nearby plant's full-shift result.
**Take** funded cutter training only with paid guarded trainer practice.
**Apply** after actual cuts only for posted safe local packaging leads at bill-covering pay and workable shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic lost hours, while able to check working equipment first.
S1.quote: I will not leave a good wage for an overtime estimate.
fieldNote: Her **steady approach** seeks real full-shift camera results before she accepts a change to the roster.
The **course and job** are distinct: paid safe practical training needs an offered place; applications require actual cuts and posted adequate terms.

steps.text: Compare proposed cutter roster with pay slips and full-shift camera evidence
Take cutter course if funded paid guarded trainer place offered
Apply after base-hour cuts to posted safe nearby packaging leads if pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband that AGI can plan carton runs in 2028, while capable robots able to change dies and clear board jams arrive around 2031. I would want the plant to name the paid jobs that remain before the new line goes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of the cutter crew to go when a robot can set and clear the press itself. My high wage may be hard to match even with several factories nearby, and Arun's heating work could also change later. Eleven months saved is substantial, but I would lie awake working out what happens after it is used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone the new car before signing the finance papers and put part of each newly paid wage into a cash reserve. I would ask the owner for written notice, then apply after lost cutter hours only to posted nearby packaging jobs with safe duties, a base rate that covers our mortgage and shifts that fit school pickup. If no such job opens, I would keep any paid press shifts while checking actual openings at other local factories; I would not resign for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the size of the wage I might lose, though I have room to search. An eleven-month reserve cannot become an eleventh year of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the children about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them the old car is safe for now and that we are keeping money for the mortgage while jobs change. A delayed car is easier to explain than an unpaid house bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes another factory posting real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notice needs a base wage, an address and shift hours before I apply. If it is only a recruiter saying there may be work later, I would keep earning at the carton cutter.

say: I would separate **2028 order planning** from cutter robots arriving around 2031.
I would demand **written retained jobs** before the plant changes the press.
think: I expect **most cutter hours** to vanish after capable robots arrive.
Eleven months saved cannot replace my **high wage** indefinitely, even with local options.
do: **Postpone** the new car before finance and save fresh paid wages.
**Ask** for written job notice before the line changes.
**Apply** after cutter cuts to posted safe nearby work only at mortgage-covering base pay and family-compatible shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major pay loss and sleepless reserve calculations.
S2.quote: An eleven-month reserve cannot become an eleventh year of pay.
fieldNote: She expects **physical cutter robots** around 2031 to remove the crew after AGI reaches scheduling in 2028.
The **new car delay** protects cash; external applications require lost hours and actual safe postings with sufficient wages and school-compatible shifts.

steps.text: Postpone new car before signing finance papers
Save part of newly paid cutter wages in cash reserve
Apply after cuts to posted safe nearby factory work if base pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI may schedule cartons in 2031, while capable robots could change the physical dies around 2034. Five years gives the factory time to pay for a proper test and keep apprenticeships open while people still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots reach the cutter. A quality-assurance post might suit my eye for a weak crease, but I would not call a new title secure without a posted wage. With full shifts, Arun and I could add to the reserve before the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save a new amount from each full paid quarter after the mortgage. If the employer offers a recognised carton-quality certificate with fees covered, paid release and a guarded practical place, I would enroll and practise measuring crease strength. After qualifying, if cutter hours fall, I would apply only for a posted local quality post with stop authority, a base wage and shift compatible with our bills and school pickup; without the course, I would look for posted packaging lead work on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the later roster, but five years gives us choices that are written down. I could stand another course if it taught me on actual board instead of slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a weak crease?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would fold and pull the first test carton, measure where the board tears and stop a bad run. The assessor must see me reject it at a guarded cutter before I trust the qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the quality post has no stop authority?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not take it, even if the title sounds senior. If a bad medicine box goes out under my name, I need the authority to hold the roll.

say: I would keep **paid apprenticeships** during the five-year warning.
A **quality role** needs a real wage and authority to reject bad cartons.
think: A **quality post** may fit my skill, but its wage must be posted.
Full paid shifts could grow our **cash reserve** before robots reach the cutter.
do: **Save** newly earned full-quarter money after mortgage bills.
**Enroll** in carton-quality study only with covered fees, paid release and guarded practice.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts to posted local quality, or suitable packaging lead work without a course.
feel: **Anxious** about later paid hours, with time to verify a practical route.
S3.quote: If a bad medicine box goes out under my name, I need the authority to hold the roll.
fieldNote: She will **measure real cartons** in a recognised course only with paid release, covered fees and guarded assessment.
The **quality application** requires a posted wage, safe stop authority and school-compatible shift; a separate lead search covers no course.

Enroll in recognised carton-quality course if fees paid and guarded paid place offered
Apply for posted local quality if qualified and cut, stop authority pay and pickup fit
Search posted safe packaging leads if no course, base pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop AGI might plan medicine cartons in 2036, while capable robots can change dies around 2039. A decade is enough to teach young operators how to inspect a real carton and to make wage terms clear before anyone loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when the robots reach the cutter. The children may be grown, but the mortgage might still be there and Arun's work may change. Our current wages and eleven-month reserve make the next few years sound, so I can test options without running from the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the cutter and make extra mortgage payments from newly earned overtime after ordinary bills. I would ask the local college which carton-quality certificate employers accept, then enroll only if a recognised place is offered with paid release, covered fees and guarded practical work. After qualifying, if cutter hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local quality jobs whose base pay and shifts cover our household costs; I would not leave before a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant roster, but secure in what we earn now. I want to finish a real test before I teach my children to trust a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your savings to start a packaging firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would want paying customers and a separate household reserve before buying equipment. A new cutter would cost money to guard and maintain, not only to purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a carton in their hands and ask them to find a weak fold before we open a screen. A young operator learns judgment by stopping one bad medicine-carton roll in time.

I would keep **hands-on apprenticeships** so younger staff can judge real cartons.

feel: **Uneasy** about distant cutter changes while current household income is sound.
S4.quote: A young operator learns judgment by stopping one bad medicine-carton roll in time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove most cutter shifts while our children still need us. Written notice, an offered paid practical qualification and posted safe nearby work at enough base pay would help. I would want the job hours in the offer, not in a recruiter’s guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs a medicine carton after the cutter is changed. A machine can print a neat label on a box that will not stay shut. Somebody needs paid authority to stop that roll before it reaches a pharmacy.

headlineQuote: A machine can print a neat label on a box that will not stay shut.
portrait: **Priya**, 43, leads a medicine-carton cutter with a two-year technical diploma and high practical skill.
She and her **heating-repair husband** Arun support two schoolchildren and a mortgage on high operator pay with eleven months saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** for manuals after others test it, and favours paid apprenticeships and clear personal responsibility for defects.
Fast **2031 cutter robots** alarm her about high-wage loss; longer warnings permit accepted practical training, new savings and real job searches.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable cutter robots around 2031 and remove most of her well-paid shifts.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written notice**, an offered funded practical qualification and posted safe nearby work at bill-covering base pay.
